steps.heading: Honeytokens Catch Attackers
steps.body:
A honeytoken is a fake credential, account, or object that has no legitimate business use — its only job is to scream when touched. In Active Directory, this means planting user accounts, SPNs, or Group Policy objects that real admins would never query. The moment an attacker's enumeration script trips over one, you know the network is compromised.

Think of it like a dye pack in a bank vault. The cash is fake, but the ink is real. Any attacker worth their salt runs BloodHound or PowerView across your domain — and those tools are indiscriminate. They'll enumerate everything, including your traps.

Honeytokens don't stop attacks. They detect them at the recon phase, before the attacker has pivoted or exfiltrated anything. That detection window is gold.

steps.heading: How AD Honeytokens Work
steps.body:
Active Directory logs every LDAP query, Kerberos ticket request, and object access — if you configure auditing correctly. A honeytoken account works by having Windows Security auditing fire an event (ID 4768 for TGT requests, 4769 for service tickets, 4625 for failed logins) whenever anyone interacts with it.

The key properties of a good AD honeytoken: it looks real (realistic name, plausible description, maybe a stale password-last-set date), it is never used by any legitimate process, and it has auditing configured to alert on any access. A user named 'svc_backup_old' with a 3-year-old password and Domain Admin group membership is catnip for attackers running privilege enumeration.

For Kerberoastable honeytokens, you assign a Service Principal Name (SPN) to the account. Any attacker running Rubeus or GetUserSPNs.py will request a TGT for it — and that TGT request is logged with the requester's IP and username. You've just tagged your attacker without them knowing.

steps.heading: Creating a Honeytoken Account via PowerShell
steps.body: This script creates a convincing honeytoken user in AD, assigns an SPN to make it Kerberoastable, and enables object-level auditing so any access fires a Windows Security event.
steps.code:
# Requires: ActiveDirectory module, Domain Admin rights
# Purpose: Deploy a Kerberoastable honeytoken account with auditing

Import-Module ActiveDirectory

$HoneyName   = "svc_legacybackup"          # Looks like a real service account
$HoneyDN     = "CN=svc_legacybackup,OU=ServiceAccounts,DC=corp,DC=local"
$FakePass    = ConvertTo-SecureString "Backup2019!Legacy" -AsPlainText -Force

# Create the account — disabled so it can never actually authenticate normally
New-ADUser -Name $HoneyName `
           -SamAccountName $HoneyName `
           -AccountPassword $FakePass `
           -PasswordNeverExpires $true `
           -Enabled $false `
           -Description "Legacy backup service - DO NOT DELETE"

# Assign an SPN: this makes it Kerberoastable by any domain user
Set-ADUser -Identity $HoneyName -ServicePrincipalNames @{Add="MSSQLSvc/legacy-bkp01.corp.local:1433"}

# Enable auditing: log ALL access attempts on this object
# Get the object's ACL and add a SACL (System ACL) audit entry
$Acl = Get-Acl -Path "AD:\$HoneyDN"
$AuditRule = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectoryAuditRule(
    [System.Security.Principal.SecurityIdentifier]"S-1-1-0",  # Everyone
    [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectoryRights]::GenericAll,
    [System.Security.AccessControl.AuditFlags]::Success
)
$Acl.AddAuditRule($AuditRule)
Set-Acl -Path "AD:\$HoneyDN" -AclObject $Acl

Write-Host "[+] Honeytoken deployed: $HoneyName" -ForegroundColor Green
Write-Host "[+] SPN registered — account is now Kerberoastable" -ForegroundColor Green

steps.context: Using the Set-ADUser cmdlet, add a ServicePrincipalName to a user named "svc_legacybackup". Fill in the missing cmdlet name. The parameter is -ServicePrincipalNames @{Add="HTTP/fake.corp.local"}. Type only the cmdlet: "Set-ADUser".

steps.heading: SIEM Alert Rule for Honeytoken Access
steps.body: Deploying the account is half the job. Here's a PowerShell script that parses Windows Security event logs and fires an alert whenever Event ID 4769 (Kerberos service ticket) targets your honeytoken's SPN — run this on your SIEM forwarder or as a scheduled task.
steps.code:
# Monitor Security event log for Kerberos TGS requests targeting the honeytoken
# Event 4769: A Kerberos service ticket was requested
# Run as: Scheduled Task or forwarded via WEF to SIEM

$HoneySPN      = "MSSQLSvc/legacy-bkp01.corp.local:1433"  # Must match exactly
$AlertEmail    = "soc@corp.local"
$LookbackMins  = 5   # Check last 5 minutes on each run

$StartTime = (Get-Date).AddMinutes(-$LookbackMins)

# Filter Security log for Kerberos service ticket events
$Events = Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
    LogName   = "Security"
    Id        = 4769                   # Kerberos Service Ticket Operations
    StartTime = $StartTime
} -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

foreach ($Event in $Events) {
    $Xml     = [xml]$Event.ToXml()
    $SPN     = $Xml.Event.EventData.Data | Where-Object { $_.Name -eq "ServiceName" } | Select-Object -ExpandProperty "#text"
    $Client  = $Xml.Event.EventData.Data | Where-Object { $_.Name -eq "ClientAddress" } | Select-Object -ExpandProperty "#text"
    $Account = $Xml.Event.EventData.Data | Where-Object { $_.Name -eq "TargetUserName" } | Select-Object -ExpandProperty "#text"

    if ($SPN -like "*legacy-bkp01*") {   # Honeytoken SPN matched
        $Body = "HONEYTOKEN TRIGGERED`nSPN: $SPN`nRequester: $Account`nSource IP: $Client`nTime: $($Event.TimeCreated)"
        Write-Warning $Body
        # Send-MailMessage -To $AlertEmail -Subject "[ALERT] Honeytoken Kerberoast" -Body $Body -SmtpServer "smtp.corp.local"
    }
}

steps.heading: Filter for the Right Event ID
steps.context: In the Get-WinEvent FilterHashtable, you need to filter for Kerberos service ticket events. Fill in the correct Windows Security Event ID for a Kerberos service ticket request. The value is the integer "4769".

steps.heading: Gotchas & Opsec Mistakes
steps.body:
The most common failure: your honeytoken looks fake. If the account has a creation date of today, a generic description, and has never had a login — a seasoned attacker running BloodHound with custom Cypher queries may spot it. Age your accounts. Set a plausible PasswordLastSet date using Set-ADUser -PasswordLastSet and manipulate the attribute directly via ADSI if needed.

Second trap: no one monitors the alerts. A honeytoken that fires into a log nobody reads is security theater. Wire it into your SIEM with a P1 alert. Honeytoken alerts should have near-zero false positive rate — if one fires, treat it as a confirmed intrusion, not a maybe.

Third: don't create only one. An attacker who trips one and gets no follow-on compromise may realize it was a trap. Spread multiple honeytokens across different OUs, service account naming conventions, and privilege levels. Make them part of the AD landscape, not obvious outliers.

Finally: Kerberoastable honeytokens with weak passwords are a double-edged sword. If the attacker cracks the hash offline, they get nothing — the account is disabled and has no real access. But make sure it truly has no access, or you've built your own backdoor.

steps.heading: Disable the Honeytoken Account
steps.context: After creating the account with New-ADUser, you must disable it so it cannot be used for actual authentication. Use the Set-ADUser cmdlet with the -Identity "svc_legacybackup" and the parameter "-Enabled $false". Type only the cmdlet name: "Set-ADUser".

A) Reset the honeytoken account's password
B) Isolate the source IP's host and begin IR triage

steps.heading: ATT&CK as Code
steps.body:
The MITRE ATT&CK framework is a structured catalog of adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) — but it's just a wiki until you automate it. Purple team operators write tooling that executes specific TTPs on demand: run T1059.001 (PowerShell execution), log what EDR catches, compare against what it should catch. Rinse, repeat across 200 techniques.

Go is the right language for this. It compiles to a single static binary, runs on Windows and Linux without dependencies, and its concurrency model (goroutines) lets you execute multiple TTPs in parallel while collecting telemetry. Writing TTP automation in Go means your simulation engine is a single file drop — no Python interpreter, no DLL hell.

This module builds the core of that engine: a dispatcher that maps ATT&CK technique IDs to Go functions, executes them, and returns structured results you can feed into a reporting pipeline.

steps.heading: TTP Dispatcher Architecture
steps.body:
The architecture is a function registry: a map[string]func() TTPResult where the key is the ATT&CK technique ID (e.g. "T1082") and the value is the function that executes it. At runtime, your engine iterates a list of requested technique IDs, looks each one up in the registry, and executes it — capturing stdout, stderr, error state, and timing.

Each TTP function returns a TTPResult struct: technique ID, whether it executed successfully, any output collected, and a timestamp. This structured output is what gets serialized to JSON for your SIEM or report generator.

Concurrency is handled with goroutines and a WaitGroup. You fire each TTP in its own goroutine, collect results through a channel, and join at the end. The engine doesn't care what the TTP does — it just runs it and records the outcome. That separation of concerns is what makes the engine extensible.

steps.heading: TTP Registry and Result Types
steps.body: Here's the foundational data model and registry for the ATT&CK automation engine — the types and the map that wires technique IDs to execution functions.

steps.heading: Define the TTPResult Struct Field

type TTPResult struct {
	TechniqueID string
	Name        string
	Success     bool
	Output      string

steps.heading: Concurrent TTP Dispatcher
steps.body: This is the engine's dispatcher: it accepts a slice of technique IDs, fires each one in a goroutine, collects results through a channel, and returns them all once every goroutine completes.

steps.heading: Increment the WaitGroup
steps.context: Before launching each goroutine in the Dispatch function, you must increment the WaitGroup counter. Call the Add method on the WaitGroup variable named "wg" with argument 1. Type exactly: "wg.Add(1)".

steps.heading: Gotchas, Timing & EDR
steps.body:
The biggest mistake in TTP automation: running everything at full speed and wondering why EDR catches it all. Real adversaries introduce jitter. Build a configurable delay — even 500ms between technique executions changes the behavioral signature enough to evade time-based correlation rules. A time.Sleep(time.Duration(rand.Intn(maxJitter)) * time.Millisecond) before each dispatch is not optional in a real purple team tool.

Second gotcha: your goroutines share nothing by default, but exec.Command inherits the parent process's environment. If you're testing credential-based techniques, the test harness's own credentials bleed into subprocesses. Use exec.Cmd.Env to explicitly set a clean environment.

Third: the Registry map in Go is not goroutine-safe for writes. If you're dynamically loading techniques at runtime (e.g. from a plugin directory), protect the registry with a sync.RWMutex — read-lock during dispatch, write-lock during registration. For static registries this doesn't matter, but the moment you add hot-reload, you have a race condition.

Finally: log everything to a structured format (JSON, not printf). Your purple team report is built from these logs. An unstructured output means manual triage. Use encoding/json to marshal TTPResult directly.

steps.heading: Serialize Result to JSON
steps.context: After collecting results in Dispatch, serialize a single TTPResult variable named "r" to JSON using the standard library. Use the function "json.Marshal" passing "r" as the argument, capturing both return values into "data" and "err". Type exactly: "data, err := json.Marshal(r)".

steps.heading: Knowledge Check
steps.question:
Your ATT&CK automation engine fires T1082, T1057, and T1016 as concurrent goroutines. After calling wg.Wait() and close(results), you range over the results channel to build your output slice. In a test run, you notice results sometimes arrive in a different order than the techniques were dispatched. What is the correct interpretation?

A) There is a race condition — the WaitGroup is misconfigured
B) This is expected — goroutine scheduling is non-deterministic
C) The channel buffer is too small and dropping results
D) You must use a mutex to enforce ordering
options: There is a race condition — the WaitGroup is misconfigured
This is expected — goroutine scheduling is non-deterministic
The channel buffer is too small and is dropping results
A mutex is required to enforce result ordering
steps.hint: Recall how Go schedules goroutines and whether the dispatcher makes any guarantees about execution order versus completion order.

steps.heading: What You're Building
steps.body:
This is the capstone. You're assembling a full-stack breach simulation engine in Go: a component that plans a multi-stage attack chain (recon → initial access → persistence → exfil), executes each stage as ATT&CK-mapped TTP functions, captures telemetry at every step, and produces a structured JSON report mapping what executed against what a defender should have caught.

This is what commercial tools like Atomic Red Team, Caldera, and BAS (Breach and Attack Simulation) platforms do — except you're building it from primitives. You understand every line.

The engine has four layers: a Scenario definition (ordered list of stages with technique IDs), a Dispatcher (concurrent TTP executor from the last module), a Telemetry collector (structured logging of every execution), and a Reporter (JSON output of the full breach chain with pass/fail per technique). By the end of this module, you can drop a single Go binary on a test host, run a simulated APT campaign, and get a machine-readable report.

steps.heading: Scenario & Stage Data Model
steps.body:
A Scenario is a named, ordered sequence of Stages. Each Stage maps to an ATT&CK tactic (e.g. TA0002 Execution) and contains one or more technique IDs to run. Stages run sequentially — you don't move to Persistence until Initial Access completes. Within a stage, techniques run concurrently via the dispatcher.

The Scenario struct holds metadata (name, author, target description) and a slice of Stage structs. Each Stage has a tactic label, a slice of technique IDs, and a StopOnFailure flag — if any technique in the stage fails and that flag is set, the engine aborts the chain. This mirrors real adversary behavior: if you can't get execution, you don't bother trying to persist.

The Report struct is the output: it mirrors the Scenario structure but each technique entry is replaced with a TTPResult from the dispatcher. The report gets serialized to JSON at the end, with a top-level summary field: total techniques attempted, succeeded, failed, and total wall-clock duration.

steps.heading: Scenario Definition and Engine Core

steps.heading: Extending the Engine Safely
steps.body:
You now have a working breach simulation engine. Here's what separates a toy from a production purple team tool:

Technique isolation: each TTPFunc should run in a subprocess or sandboxed context where possible. A technique that panics shouldn't take down the entire engine. Wrap every dispatch in a recover() block and convert panics to failed TTPResults.

Detection mapping: extend TTPResult with a DetectionExpected field — a list of SIEM rule IDs or alert names that should fire for this technique. After the run, your report shows not just what executed, but what detections were and weren't triggered. That gap analysis is the whole point of purple teaming.

Cleanup hooks: every technique that creates artifacts (files, registry keys, scheduled tasks) needs a matching cleanup function. Add a Cleanup TTPFunc field to your registry entry and run it after the stage completes, regardless of success. Leave the target host in the state you found it.

Rate limiting and jitter: add a global config struct with MinJitter and MaxJitter duration fields. The dispatcher sleeps a random duration in that range before each technique. Without jitter, your engine looks like a scanner to behavioral EDR — and you've just tested whether defenders can catch a noisy script kiddie, not a real APT.

steps.context: Extend the TTPResult struct with a field to store expected detection rule IDs. Add a field named "DetectionsExpected" of type "[]string". Type exactly: "DetectionsExpected []string".

steps.heading: Variables Are Named Memory
steps.body:
A variable is a named location in memory that holds a value. When you write x = 42 in Python, the interpreter allocates space for an integer object and binds the name x to it. This is different from a language like C, where the variable IS the memory location — but understanding the model matters because it explains why bugs happen.

Every variable has three things: a name (how you refer to it in code), a type (what kind of value it holds — integer, string, list), and a value (the actual data). In Python, the type is attached to the value, not the variable — you can rebind x to a string after it held an integer. In Go or C, the type is fixed at declaration time.

Why does this matter for security? Buffer overflows happen when you write more data into a memory location than its type allows. Type confusion bugs happen when code assumes a variable holds one type but it holds another. Understanding variables at this level is the foundation of understanding every memory-safety vulnerability you'll ever exploit or defend against.

steps.heading: Types, Values & Memory Layout
steps.body:
Python's built-in types: int (arbitrary precision integer), float (64-bit IEEE 754), str (immutable Unicode string), bool (True/False, subtype of int), bytes (raw byte sequence), list (mutable ordered sequence), dict (hash map), None (null singleton).

Memory allocation in Python is managed by the interpreter. Small integers (-5 to 256) are cached — Python pre-allocates objects for them and reuses them, so id(1) == id(1) is always True. Strings are interned similarly. This is mostly invisible but bites you when you use 'is' instead of '==' for equality — 'is' compares memory addresses, not values.

For security-relevant memory work, bytes is what you'll use constantly — shellcode, network payloads, file parsing. Know that bytes objects are immutable; if you need to mutate a byte buffer in-place, use bytearray. The difference matters when you're building exploit payloads or parsing binary protocols.

steps.heading: Variables, Types & Bytes in Python
steps.body: This snippet demonstrates variable declaration, type inspection, and bytes manipulation — the primitives you'll use in every security tool you write.
steps.code:
# Python variable fundamentals — with security-relevant context

# Integer — Python ints are arbitrary precision (no overflow in pure Python)
port = 8080
print(type(port))          # <class 'int'>

# String — immutable, always Unicode in Python 3
host = "192.168.1.1"

# Bytes — raw binary data; essential for network/exploit work
shellcode = b"\x90\x90\x90\xcc"   # 3 NOPs + INT3 breakpoint
print(len(shellcode))             # 4 — each \xNN is one byte

# Bytearray — mutable bytes; use when you need to patch bytes in-place
buf = bytearray(b"\x00" * 16)    # 16 null bytes — simulating a buffer
buf[0] = 0x41                    # Patch first byte to 'A' (0x41)
buf[1] = 0x42                    # Patch second byte to 'B'
print(buf[:4])                    # bytearray(b'AB\x00\x00')

# Type conversion — critical when parsing binary protocols
hex_val = "0x41"                  # String representation of a hex value
int_val = int(hex_val, 16)        # Convert hex string to integer: 65
char_val = chr(int_val)           # Convert integer to character: 'A'
print(f"{hex_val} -> {int_val} -> {char_val}")

# None — Python's null; check for it explicitly
result = None
if result is None:                # Use 'is', not '==' for None checks
    print("No result yet")

steps.heading: Declare a Bytes Variable
steps.context: Declare a variable named "payload" and assign it a bytes literal containing two NOP bytes (\x90) followed by a breakpoint (\xcc). The value must be exactly "b'\x90\x90\xcc'". Type exactly: "payload = b'\x90\x90\xcc'".

steps.heading: Memory Allocation Patterns
steps.body: This snippet shows Python's integer caching, the difference between 'is' and '==', and how to inspect memory addresses — directly relevant when reasoning about object identity in exploit tooling.
steps.code:
import sys

# Python caches small integers (-5 to 256) — same object in memory
a = 256
b = 256
print(a is b)    # True — same cached object
print(id(a))     # Memory address of the integer 256

# Large integers are NOT cached — different objects
x = 1000
y = 1000
print(x is y)    # False — two separate objects (in CPython, usually)
print(x == y)    # True — same value

# Memory size of objects — useful for understanding payload sizing
print(sys.getsizeof(0))              # 28 bytes — Python int overhead
print(sys.getsizeof(b"A" * 100))    # 133 bytes — bytes object overhead + 100
print(sys.getsizeof(bytearray(100))) # 157 bytes — bytearray has extra overhead

# Mutable vs immutable — why this matters for buffer building
original = b"\x41\x42\x43"         # Immutable bytes
try:
    original[0] = 0x44              # TypeError: bytes object does not support item assignment
except TypeError as e:
    print(f"Can't mutate bytes: {e}")

mutable = bytearray(original)       # Convert to mutable bytearray
mutable[0] = 0x44                   # Now we can patch it
print(bytes(mutable))               # b'DAC' — first byte patched

steps.heading: Convert Bytes to Bytearray
steps.context: Given an immutable bytes variable named "raw" containing b'\x41\x42\x43', convert it to a mutable bytearray and assign the result to a variable named "buf". Use the "bytearray()" constructor. Type exactly: "buf = bytearray(raw)".

steps.heading: Scope, Mutability & Gotchas
steps.body:
Python has three main scopes: local (inside a function), global (module level), and built-in (Python's own names). The LEGB rule — Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in — is the order Python searches for a name. If you assign to a variable inside a function without declaring it global, Python creates a new local variable and the outer one is untouched. Miss this and your exploit script silently fails to update state.

Mutable default arguments are a classic Python trap. def f(buf=[]): buf.append(1) — the list is created once at function definition time, not on each call. Every call shares the same list object. In security tooling, this can cause payload contamination across calls. Always use None as the default and create the mutable inside the function.

The bytes vs str distinction bites everyone: socket.send() needs bytes, not str. If you pass a string, you get a TypeError at runtime. Always encode strings explicitly: data.encode('utf-8') or use a bytes literal. Mixing them silently was a Python 2 behavior — Python 3 is strict, which is correct, but requires discipline.

steps.heading: Encode a String to Bytes
steps.context: You have a string variable named "cmd" containing the value "whoami". Convert it to a UTF-8 bytes object and assign the result to a variable named "payload". Use the string method ".encode()" with argument "'utf-8'". Type exactly: "payload = cmd.encode('utf-8')".

steps.heading: Control Flow Is Execution Logic
steps.body:
Control flow determines which lines of code run, how many times, and under what conditions. Every program — from a login form to a shellcode loader — is fundamentally a control flow problem. Understanding it deeply means you can read unfamiliar code and predict its behavior without running it. That skill is equally useful for writing exploits and for reverse engineering ones.

Python has three primary control flow mechanisms: conditionals (if/elif/else), loops (for and while), and exception handling (try/except). Each has idiomatic uses and common misuses. A for loop that should be a list comprehension, or a while loop with a missing break, are bugs that security tools inherit from general Python code. Know the difference.

In security contexts, control flow errors are vulnerability classes: off-by-one errors in loop bounds, unchecked conditionals on authentication paths, infinite loops in parsers. Writing correct control flow is not just style — it's the difference between a working tool and a segfault.

steps.heading: Loops, Conditionals & Iteration
steps.body:
Python's for loop iterates over any iterable — lists, ranges, bytes, file lines, generator expressions. range(n) gives you integers 0 to n-1. range(start, stop, step) gives you a slice of integers. Iterating over bytes gives you integers (each byte as an int), not characters — remember this when parsing binary data.

The while loop runs as long as its condition is true. The canonical network tool pattern is while True with a break on a sentinel value — reading from a socket until the connection closes. The danger: forget the break condition and you've written an infinite loop that locks your process.

Conditionals in Python are clean but have traps. Truthiness: empty string, 0, None, [], {}, b'' are all falsy. A check like if data: passes for any non-empty, non-zero value. This is convenient until your code needs to distinguish between 0 and None — then you must use explicit comparisons (if data is not None, if data != 0). In protocol parsers, this distinction is the difference between correctly handling a zero-length payload and silently dropping it.

steps.heading: Loops and Conditionals in Python
steps.body: This snippet demonstrates the core control flow patterns you'll use in network tools and binary parsers — including the byte iteration trap and while-True socket pattern.
steps.code:
# Control flow fundamentals — security tool context

# for loop over a range — port scanning range
for port in range(1, 1025):        # 1 to 1024 inclusive
    if port == 80 or port == 443:  # Conditional inside loop
        print(f"Web port: {port}")

# Iterating over bytes — each element is an int, not a char
shellcode = b"\x41\x42\x90\x90\xcc"
for byte in shellcode:
    print(hex(byte), end=" ")      # 0x41 0x42 0x90 0x90 0xcc
print()                            # Newline after byte dump

# enumerate() — when you need both index and value
for i, byte in enumerate(shellcode):
    if byte == 0x90:               # Find NOP sled positions
        print(f"NOP at offset {i}")

# while True with break — canonical socket read pattern
import socket
def read_until(sock, delimiter=b"\n", max_bytes=4096):
    buf = b""
    while True:                    # Run until break
        chunk = sock.recv(1)       # Read one byte at a time
        if not chunk:              # Empty bytes = connection closed
            break
        buf += chunk
        if delimiter in buf:       # Found the delimiter
            break
        if len(buf) >= max_bytes:  # Safety: prevent unbounded read
            break
    return buf

steps.heading: Loop Bugs & Off-By-One Errors
steps.body:
Off-by-one errors are the most common loop bug and a genuine vulnerability class. range(n) gives 0 to n-1 — that final -1 catches people constantly. If you mean to process n items and write range(1, n) instead of range(n), you silently skip the first item. In a byte parser, that skipped byte corrupts every subsequent offset.

The classic off-by-one in a while loop: while i <= len(buf) instead of while i < len(buf). On the last iteration, buf[i] accesses index len(buf), which raises an IndexError in Python — but in C, it silently reads one byte past the buffer. That's a read primitive in an exploit.

Break and continue are your tools for loop control. break exits the entire loop; continue skips to the next iteration. Misplacing a break inside a nested conditional — inside an if inside a for — exits only the for loop, not any outer while. If your loop isn't terminating when you expect, trace every break statement and verify which loop it actually exits.

List comprehensions and generator expressions replace most simple loops in idiomatic Python. [hex(b) for b in shellcode] is cleaner and faster than a for loop building a list. But they can't contain break or continue — if you need those, use a regular loop.

steps.heading: Knowledge Check
steps.question:
You're parsing a binary buffer where each record is 4 bytes long. You write:

    for i in range(1, len(buf), 4):
        record = buf[i:i+4]

Your test buffer has 12 bytes. You expect 3 records but only get 2. What is the bug?

A) The slice buf[i:i+4] should be buf[i:i+3]
B) range() should start at 0, not 1 — the first record is being skipped
C) You should use a while loop for binary parsing
D) len(buf) should be len(buf) - 4 to avoid the last record
options: The slice buf[i:i+4] should be buf[i:i+3]
range() starts at 1 — the first record is being skipped
Binary parsing requires a while loop, not for
len(buf) should be len(buf) - 4
